questions_and_answers.question_text: Why is -de not used after jiějie in 6A?
What idea does the pattern yuè...yuè... express?
What does the pattern express when lái is used in the first blank?
Why is zài used in 6B even though the action isn't happening right now?
What is the literal meaning of pīnmìng?
Write the Chinese for "The more friends you have, the better."
Write the Chinese for "Things are getting more and more expensive."

answers.answer_text: Dōngxi yuè lái yuè guì le.
Having two -de phrases in a row before a noun — the way around it is to keep only the last -de.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Which marker often ends a sentence containing zài?
Write the Chinese for "The more he talked, the madder he got."

articles.text:
6. A: Nǐ jiějie yīxué fāngmiànde    Your sister is getting more and more
      shū yuè lái yuè duō le!        medical books!
   B: Shì a, tā zài pīnmìng xué yī  Yes, she's studying medicine with all
      ne.                            her energy.

Notes on No. 6

nǐ jiějie yīxué fāngmiànde shū: "your sister's medical books." To say just "your sister's books" you put a -de on jiějie: Nǐ jiějiede shū. But -de is NOT used after jiějie in 6A. This is because of the modifying phrase yīxué fāngmiànde, which ends in -de. To have TWO -de phrases in a row before a noun is often considered stylistically BAD; the way to get around it is to keep only the LAST -de.

yuè lái yuè duō le: The pattern yuè...yuè... is used to express the idea "THE MORE...THE MORE...." Fill in the blanks with verbs.

Péngyou yuè duō yuè hǎo.         The more friends you have, the better.
Dìtú yuè dà yuè qīngchu.         The larger a map is, the clearer it is.
Wǒ yuè xiǎng yuè pà.             The more I thought about it, the more
                                 frightened I got.
Tā yuè shuō yuè shēngqì.         The more he talked, the madder he got.
Nèipiān wénzhāng xiěde hěn bù    The article is very unclear. The more
qīngchu, nǐ yuè kàn yuè bù dǒng. you read it, the less you understand.

When the verb LÁI is used in the first blank, the whole phrase expresses "INCREASINGLY..." or "...-er and ...-er":

Huáng Tàitaide nǚér yuè lái yuè  Mrs. Huáng's daughter is getting
piàoliang le.                    prettier all the time.
Dōngxi yuè lái yuè guì le.       Things are getting more and more
                                 expensive.

zài: Zài is the marker of ONGOING ACTION. Note that zài is used in 6B even though the action of studying is not necessarily going on at this very second, but only at intervals. She might not be studying right when this sentence is said, but she still is going to medical school.

zài...ne: Sentences with zài often end in ne, the marker of absence of change or lack of completion.

pīnmìng: "with all one's might, for all one is worth, desperately, like mad." Pīnmìng means literally "to risk one's life" or "to defy death." One translation which captures the spirit is "knocking oneself out."

Shìqing tài duō, tā pīnmìngde    There's too much to do. She's working
zuò yě zuòbuwán.                 like mad and still won't finish.
